lessonTitle: Cataract, Glaucoma and Diabetic Eye Disease

blocks.text: A 61-year-old taxi driver passes his eyesight check with the better eye every year, yet has been clipping wing mirrors for months. Nothing hurts and nothing looks blurred. Chronic eye disease steals vision slowly and quietly, which is exactly why screening and recognition matter.

blocks.title: Cataract
blocks.text: Any opacity of the crystalline lens that reduces vision. The lens normally focuses light because it is transparent and flexible; with age, proteins aggregate and the lens clouds. Types include nuclear sclerosis, cortical and posterior subcapsular. Risk factors: age, diabetes, corticosteroids (topical or systemic), smoking, UV exposure, previous eye trauma or inflammation, and congenital causes.

blocks.markdown:
**Clinical features of cataract.** Gradual, painless blurring; glare, especially from headlights or low sun; reduced contrast; faded colours; and in nuclear sclerosis a myopic shift (the lens becomes more refractive, so reading may temporarily improve). Monocular double vision may occur. On examination, the red reflex looks dark or patchy through an ophthalmoscope held at arm's length, and the opacity is seen at the slit lamp.

**Treatment** is surgical when vision interferes with daily life, such as driving or reading: no single acuity cut-off decides it. The standard operation is *phacoemulsification* (ultrasound breaks the lens nucleus, which is removed through a small incision) and implantation of an *intraocular lens*, usually as a day case under topical or local anaesthesia. Complications: posterior capsule opacification (months to years later; treated by YAG laser capsulotomy), posterior capsule rupture, cystoid macular oedema, retinal detachment, and rarely *endophthalmitis*, an intraocular infection presenting days after surgery with pain, falling vision and a hypopyon, which needs same-day specialist care.

**Glaucoma: the aqueous circuit.** The ciliary body makes aqueous humour, which flows through the pupil into the anterior chamber and drains through the trabecular meshwork to Schlemm's canal (and in smaller part by the uveoscleral route). *Intraocular pressure* (IOP) is set by production against outflow resistance. A statistical normal range is about 10 to 21 mmHg, though glaucoma can occur at lower pressures and many people with higher pressure never develop it.

blocks.title: Glaucoma
blocks.text: A chronic optic neuropathy characterised by progressive loss of retinal ganglion cells, with cupping of the optic disc and corresponding visual field loss. IOP is the main *modifiable* risk factor. In primary open-angle glaucoma the drainage angle is open but outflow resistance in the trabecular meshwork is raised.

blocks.markdown:
**How raised IOP damages the nerve.** Retinal ganglion cell axons converge on the optic disc and leave the eye through the *lamina cribrosa*, a sieve-like collagen plate. Raised pressure deforms this plate, which compresses and kinks axons and blocks axonal transport of growth factors, leading to ganglion cell death. Reduced blood supply adds to the damage: *ocular perfusion pressure* is the driving pressure for blood flow in the optic nerve head, and a common simplified estimate is given below. Axon loss thins the neuroretinal rim, so the central cup enlarges (rising cup-to-disc ratio, with notching or disc haemorrhage).

Clinically, loss starts in the **peripheral** field (arcuate scotomas, nasal step) while central acuity is kept until late, and the brain fills in gaps, so patients do not notice. Detection is by optic disc assessment, tonometry and perimetry (and OCT).

blocks.caption: $P_s$, $P_d$ systolic and diastolic blood pressure (mmHg); IOP in mmHg. The 2/3 factor is a convention for supine/sitting estimates and varies between authors.

blocks.title: Worked example: ocular perfusion pressure
blocks.prompt: A patient has blood pressure 130/80 mmHg and IOP 24 mmHg. Estimate the mean ocular perfusion pressure using the convention above.

steps.text: Scale to the eye with the 2/3 convention: 2/3 x 96.67 = 64.44 mmHg.

Interpretation: both a rise in IOP and a fall in blood pressure (such as aggressive night-time antihypertensive treatment) reduce this figure, which is why perfusion adds to the injury in some patients.

blocks.markdown: **Management of glaucoma.** The aim is to slow progression by lowering IOP; the *target* is individual and is often expressed as a percentage reduction from untreated baseline (for example 20 to 30 percent or more as damage advances), then adjusted to field progression. Options: topical prostaglandin analogues (first line in many guidelines; increase uveoscleral outflow), beta-blockers (reduce production; avoid in asthma and bradycardia), carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and alpha-agonists; selective laser trabeculoplasty; and trabeculectomy or drainage devices when drops fail. Check agent choice and dosing against current BNF and NICE guidance.

rows: Often none until late; peripheral field loss
Large cup, rim thinning, arcuate scotoma
None until late; floaters, sudden loss with bleed
Glycaemic and BP control, laser, anti-VEGF, vitrectomy
blocks.caption: Chronic causes of visual impairment compared

blocks.markdown: **Diabetic retinopathy: from pericyte to new vessel.** Chronic hyperglycaemia damages the retinal capillaries: pericyte loss and basement membrane thickening produce *microaneurysms* and leak (haemorrhages and lipid *hard exudates*), then capillary closure causes ischaemia (*cotton wool spots*, venous beading and intraretinal microvascular abnormalities), and ischaemic retina releases VEGF, driving fragile *new vessels* that bleed into the vitreous and pull on the retina. Fluid leak at the macula (*diabetic macular oedema*) is a common cause of central loss in type 2 diabetes.

rows: Microaneurysms, dot and blot haemorrhages, hard exudates
Optimise glycaemia, BP and lipids; screening
Cotton wool spots, venous beading, intraretinal microvascular abnormalities
Closer ophthalmic review; risk of progression is high
New vessels on the disc or elsewhere; vitreous haemorrhage; traction
Exudates or oedema near the fovea
blocks.caption: Stages of diabetic retinopathy (England uses R and M grades in screening; check current national grading)

blocks.title: Worked example: grading a screening photograph
blocks.prompt: A 49-year-old with type 2 diabetes has retinal photographs showing scattered dot haemorrhages and two cotton wool spots with venous beading in one quadrant; no new vessels and the macula is clear. Visual acuity is normal. Stage the disease and plan.

steps.text: Dot haemorrhages indicate microaneurysm leakage, so non-proliferative disease is present.
Cotton wool spots and venous beading show retinal ischaemia, which separates pre-proliferative (severe non-proliferative) from background disease.
There are no new vessels and the macula is clear, so this is not proliferative disease or maculopathy; acuity is normal because symptoms appear late.

Plan: refer for ophthalmic assessment (not annual routine screening), reinforce glycaemic, blood pressure and lipid control, and arrange short-interval review because progression to proliferative disease is likely. Screening matters because by the time symptoms occur the disease is advanced.

blocks.answer: Pre-proliferative diabetic retinopathy with no maculopathy; refer to the hospital eye service.

blocks.title: Why screening works
blocks.text: Diabetic retinopathy is asymptomatic until late, and treatment (laser, anti-VEGF) preserves rather than restores vision. Organised national programmes offer regular digital retinal photography with pupil dilatation to everyone with diabetes from age 12 in the UK programme; intervals depend on the grade and local policy, so check current guidance. Large rapid falls in HbA1c can transiently worsen retinopathy and need monitoring.

points: Cataract is a gradual lens opacity treated by phacoemulsification and an intraocular lens; endophthalmitis is the rare serious complication.
Raised IOP deforms the lamina cribrosa, blocks axonal transport and reduces perfusion, killing retinal ganglion cells; peripheral field loss comes first, so patients are unaware.
Diabetic retinopathy progresses from microaneurysms to ischaemia to new vessel growth, with maculopathy affecting central vision; screening detects it while vision is still normal.
Doses and treatment protocols should be checked against current BNF, NICE and national screening guidance.

questions.stem: A 77-year-old woman reports a year of gradually blurred vision and dazzle from oncoming headlights. Both pupils react normally, the red reflex on the right is dull and she has no eye pain. Which is the most appropriate definitive treatment if her symptoms affect her daily life?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: removing the opaque lens and replacing it restores vision.
distractorRationale.b: Used to lower IOP in glaucoma.
distractorRationale.d: Treatment for macular oedema or neovascular disease, not cataract.

questions.explanation: Gradual painless blur, glare and a dull red reflex indicate cataract. Surgery is offered when symptoms affect daily life, and the standard operation is phacoemulsification with an intraocular lens.

questions.stem: Four days after uncomplicated cataract surgery on his left eye, a 69-year-old man has increasing eye pain and falling vision. The eye is red and a white layer of cells is seen at the bottom of the anterior chamber. What is the most likely diagnosis and action?

options.text: Posterior capsule opacification; routine laser next month

distractorRationale.a: Correct: postoperative pain, falling vision and a hypopyon suggest intraocular infection.
distractorRationale.b: This occurs months to years later and is painless.
distractorRationale.c: Pain with falling vision and hypopyon is not expected.

questions.explanation: Pain, deteriorating vision and a hypopyon a few days after surgery are the hallmarks of endophthalmitis, an ophthalmic emergency needing urgent sampling and intravitreal antibiotics. Posterior capsule opacification is a late painless problem.

questions.stem: The decision to offer cataract surgery depends on how much the visual impairment affects the patient's daily activities, not on a single fixed acuity threshold.
questions.explanation: Cataract surgery is a functional decision made with the patient, taking in driving, reading, work and safety, along with fitness for surgery. Guidelines discourage restricting access by acuity alone.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with primary open-angle glaucoma says he has noticed no change in his sight, yet his visual field test shows marked loss. Which explanation best fits?

options.text: Peripheral field is lost first and central acuity is preserved until late, and the brain fills the gaps
Glaucoma mainly damages the macula early
Raised IOP causes pain that patients ignore
The lens is opacified, hiding the field defect

questions.correctOptionText: Peripheral field is lost first and central acuity is preserved until late, and the brain fills the gaps

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this is the natural history.
distractorRationale.b: The central field is relatively spared early.
distractorRationale.c: Chronic open-angle glaucoma is usually painless.

questions.explanation: Primary open-angle glaucoma kills ganglion cells in a pattern that first affects the mid-peripheral field, and central vision is kept until late. The patient therefore does not notice the losses, which is why case-finding by disc examination, tonometry and perimetry matters.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes where and how raised intraocular pressure damages the optic nerve?

options.text: It deforms the lamina cribrosa, compressing axons, blocking axonal transport and reducing perfusion
It tears the retinal pigment epithelium causing choroidal bleeding
It causes optic nerve inflammation behind the globe
It increases lens thickness which compresses the nerve

questions.correctOptionText: It deforms the lamina cribrosa, compressing axons, blocking axonal transport and reducing perfusion

distractorRationale.b: Not the mechanism of glaucomatous neuropathy.

questions.explanation: The optic nerve axons exit through the lamina cribrosa, which deforms under raised pressure. Axon compression, impaired axonal transport and reduced perfusion cause ganglion cell death, visible as rim thinning and a larger cup.

questions.stem: A patient has blood pressure 150/90 mmHg and intraocular pressure 30 mmHg. Using MAP = diastolic + one-third of pulse pressure and OPP = (2/3) x MAP - IOP, calculate the ocular perfusion pressure in mmHg.
questions.explanation: MAP = 90 + (150 - 90)/3 = 110 mmHg; two-thirds of this is 73.3 mmHg, and subtracting the IOP of 30 mmHg gives 43.3 mmHg. This is a convention-based estimate, and different authors use slightly different factors.

questions.stem: A man with newly diagnosed glaucoma has an untreated IOP of 26 mmHg and his clinician sets a target of a 30 percent reduction from baseline. What is the target IOP in mmHg?
questions.explanation: A 30 percent reduction means the target is 70 percent of baseline, which is 0.70 x 26 = 18.2 mmHg. Target IOPs are individual, based on baseline pressure, damage and progression, and are revised over time.

questions.stem: Retinal photographs of a 55-year-old with type 2 diabetes show cotton wool spots, venous beading and intraretinal microvascular abnormalities, but no new vessels. What is the stage of retinopathy?

distractorRationale.b: Only microaneurysms, dot haemorrhages and exudates.
distractorRationale.c: Requires new vessels on the disc or elsewhere.
distractorRationale.d: Arteriolar changes and flame haemorrhages predominate there.

questions.explanation: Cotton wool spots, venous beading and intraretinal microvascular abnormalities reflect retinal ischaemia, marking the pre-proliferative stage. Proliferative disease is defined by new vessel growth, and these patients need ophthalmic review because progression risk is high.

questions.stem: Explain why diabetic retinopathy is screened for in people with diabetes, and describe how the disease progresses from background changes to sight-threatening disease.
markingGuide: Asymptomatic until late, so vision is normal while the disease is treatable
Treatment (laser, anti-VEGF, vitrectomy) preserves vision rather than restores it
Hyperglycaemia damages capillaries: microaneurysms, haemorrhages, exudates (background)
Capillary closure leads to ischaemia: cotton wool spots, venous beading, IRMA (pre-proliferative)
VEGF drives new vessels, which bleed or cause traction (proliferative); macular oedema affects central vision at any stage
Regular dilated digital photography with referral by grade; control glycaemia, BP and lipids
questions.explanation: A full answer links the screening rationale to the long asymptomatic phase and to the effectiveness of early treatment, and traces the progression through ischaemia and VEGF-driven neovascularisation. Mentioning maculopathy shows understanding that central vision can fail early.

questions.stem: Describe how raised intraocular pressure leads to glaucomatous visual loss and list the main strategies used to lower it.
markingGuide: IOP determined by aqueous production against outflow through trabecular meshwork
Raised pressure deforms the lamina cribrosa, compressing axons and blocking axonal transport
Reduced optic nerve head perfusion contributes (OPP = 2/3 MAP - IOP)
Ganglion cell death: rim thinning, cupping, peripheral field loss first
Treatment: prostaglandin analogue, beta-blocker, CAI, alpha-agonist drops; selective laser trabeculoplasty; trabeculectomy or drainage surgery
Doses and agent choice per BNF/NICE
questions.explanation: The answer should move from outflow resistance to pressure, mechanical and vascular injury, and the characteristic disc and field changes, before listing treatments that reduce production or increase outflow.
